title: Foreign Tourists Praise Delhi Metro as Cleaner and Safer Than Western Underground Systems
excerpt: A viral video by a British travel creator comparing Delhi Metro favorably to London's Underground has renewed attention on India's expanding metro infrastructure and its affordability.
body:
• Multiple foreign tourists have praised Delhi Metro for its cleanliness, affordability, and efficiency, comparing it favorably to London's Underground and other Western transit systems
  • British travel creator Rory Porter's viral video highlighting a Rs 43 (£0.35) half-hour journey sparked a wave of international attention for India's metro network
  • Delhi Metro, which serves over 2.5 million daily riders across 250+ stations, features air-conditioned coaches, airport-style security, and women-only cars

A British Tourist's Viral Verdict

When British travel creator Rory Porter boarded the Delhi Metro for the first time in early 2026, he expected the usual big-city transit experience — crowds, confusion, and noise. What he found was the opposite.

"Okay, just Rs 43 — 0.35 pounds — for a half-hour journey. Very, very cheap. Probably one of the cheapest trains or metros I have been on in the world," Porter told his roughly 15,000 Instagram followers in a video that quickly went viral.

Porter, who has traveled to India twice, methodically walked viewers through his experience: the airport-style security checks with bag X-ray screening, the modern coaches, the air conditioning, and the conspicuous absence of overcrowding. His conclusion was blunt.

"Very efficient, lots of stations. Better than London. That is one of the best metros I have been on. Very nice, all air-conditioned, very clean, very modern."

— Rory Porter, British travel creator

Why the Video Struck a Chord

Porter's video, posted in February 2026, was picked up by multiple Indian and international news outlets within hours, according to reports from The Daily Jagran and Times Life. The footage resonated for a simple reason: international visitors rarely compare Indian infrastructure favorably to Western systems.

The video triggered a broader conversation on social media. Indian commuters shared their own positive experiences, pointing to features like women-only coaches, strong security presence, and the system's wide coverage. Transportation experts noted that such clips serve as useful mirrors for urban policymakers to gauge public perception, according to Indiascope.

Some commenters offered balanced perspectives, acknowledging gaps in last-mile connectivity and peak-hour crowding while still praising the overall system.

Delhi Metro by the Numbers

The praise is not without basis. Delhi Metro, operated by the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), is one of the largest metro networks in the world by route length. It serves the National Capital Region with over 250 stations across multiple lines, including the driverless Magenta Line with platform screen doors — features that some TripAdvisor reviewers have noted put the system "on par with rapid transit systems in Eastern Asia."

Fares start as low as Rs 10 for short distances, making it one of the most affordable urban transit options globally. The system carries over 2.5 million passengers daily and has been credited with reducing vehicular pollution and traffic congestion in one of the world's most crowded cities.

Not Just Delhi

Porter's video has prompted many Indian social media users to encourage him to try metro systems in other cities. India now operates metro networks in over a dozen cities, including Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Kolkata, Kochi, and Lucknow, with several more under construction.

The broader narrative fits into India's infrastructure push over the past decade, which has expanded metro rail, expressways, and airport capacity across the country. For members of the Indian diaspora who return periodically, the transformation of public transit is often one of the most visible markers of change.

A Useful Reality Check

Not everyone views the praise uncritically. Regular commuters note that Porter's experience during off-peak hours does not reflect the crush of rush-hour travel. Issues with last-mile connectivity — the gap between metro stations and final destinations — remain a persistent complaint.

Still, the viral moment captures something real: a public transit system that, at its best, can compete with established networks in developed economies, at a fraction of the cost.
